source: Kalyuga (2007) Expertise reversal effect and its implications for learner-tailored instruction
finding: Review of expertise reversal studies. Support that helps novices (integrated text, worked examples, animation, guidance) gets weaker or negative for more expert learners.
numbers: Conservative effect-size differences (novice effect minus expert effect) ran from 0.45 to 2.99, mid-range 1.72. More than 2200 students in the reviewed studies.
quote: The effect has been consistently replicated in many experiments
limits: Mostly cross-sectional (different people as novices and experts). SDs chosen conservatively when missing. No publication-bias check. The author is a proponent of the effect.
agent_relevance: S0: a lesson that helps a weak class can be neutral or harmful on a class the model already solves. Test per class, not globally.

source: Kalyuga et al. (1998) via Kalyuga (2007) Table 1: diagram with embedded text vs diagram only
finding: Same training material flipped sign with expertise: helped novices, hurt experts.
numbers: Operation and troubleshooting test: novices d=1.67 (N=17), experts d=-0.44 (N=30), difference 2.11. Fault-finding test: novices 1.89, experts -0.88, difference 2.77.
limits: Electrical-circuit domain, adult trainees. Secondary report of the numbers (Table 1 of the 2007 review).
agent_relevance: Full reversal exists in one domain: the extra text became redundant once the schema was built. Redundant context costs a strong model effort.

source: Kalyuga et al. (2001a,b) via Kalyuga (2007) Table 1: worked examples vs problem solving or exploration
finding: Worked examples beat problem solving for novices. For trained, more expert learners the benefit vanished or reversed.
numbers: Exp 1 (relay-circuit programs): novices d=0.90 (N=24), experts 0.23 (N=24), diff 0.67. Exp 2 (switching equations): novices -0.26, experts -0.75 (N=24 each), diff 0.49. Kalyuga 2001a Exp 2 worked examples vs exploratory learning: novices 0.69 (N=17), experts -0.33 (N=17), diff 1.02.
limits: Exp 2 shows no positive effect even for novices, only a gap. So the interaction is the claim, not a clean sign flip each time.
agent_relevance: Predicts a cross-over in a library ablation: example benefit positive on weak classes, near zero or negative on strong ones. Look for the interaction, not the sign.

source: Lee et al. (2006) and Yeung et al. (1998) via Kalyuga (2007) Table 1
finding: Reversal for representation formats and for definition placement. Iconic vs symbolic simulation differed strongly by expertise. Integrated vocabulary helped low-ability and young students and hurt high-ability and university students.
numbers: Lee 2006: novices d=0.30 (N=48), experts -1.39 (N=63), diff 2.99, the largest in the table. Yeung 1998 Exp 4-5: low vs high ability secondary students, expert effect -0.79 (N=17), diff 1.87; Exp 2-3 primary vs university, diff 0.83 and 0.66.
limits: Small cells (N=17 to 63). The largest effect sizes come from small samples, which inflates estimates.
agent_relevance: How a lesson is shown can reverse too, not only whether it is shown.

source: Reisslein et al. (2006) and Reisslein (2005) via Kalyuga (2007): fading pace by prior knowledge
finding: Backward fading and its pace depend on prior knowledge. Novices did best with example-problem pairs and slow fading. Experts did best with problem-example pairs, faded sequences, and fast or immediate transition.
numbers: Significant interactions between prior knowledge and pace on a retention posttest (engineering freshmen, circuit analysis). Experts better in fast fading and immediate transition than slow fading. Exact F and N not given in the review.
limits: Only the review text was read; effect sizes and N for this study are not reported there.
agent_relevance: Fading speed should depend on measured competence. Fade fast on strong classes, slowly on weak ones.

source: Kalyuga & Sweller (2004, 2005) and Salden et al. (2006) via Kalyuga (2007): learner-adapted instruction
finding: Adapting guidance to a rapid pretest and ongoing tests beat non-adapted instruction. Worked-out steps were gradually replaced by problem steps as expertise grew.
numbers: Knowledge gain effect size 0.46 (2004). 2005 with an efficiency indicator: knowledge gain 0.55, efficiency gain 0.69. Salden 2006 personalised task selection 0.58. Corbalan 2006 shared control: posttest 0.25, load 0.37.
limits: Effect sizes are moderate (0.25 to 0.69), well below the cross-sectional reversal differences. Lab and short training.
agent_relevance: Closest human analogue of S0 with a gate: measure ability first (rapid first-step test), then set the support level.

source: Kalyuga (2006, 2007) validation of rapid diagnostic tests, via Kalyuga (2007)
finding: A cheap first-step or rapid verification test predicts expertise well enough to route learners.
numbers: Correlations .71 and .75 with observed solution steps and verbal reports; test time cut by factors of 3.2 and 3.5 (kinematics, graph transformations). Reading comprehension: time cut by factor 3.7.
limits: Correlations are with the authors' own process measures, not with later learning gains.
agent_relevance: Supports a short probe of the model on a class before deciding whether to show lessons for that class.

source: Cooper et al. (2001), Ginns et al. (2003), Leahy & Sweller (2005) via Kalyuga (2007): imagining vs studying examples
finding: Imagining a procedure beat studying a worked example for knowledgeable learners and hurt novices. The same primary-school children flipped within two weeks of training.
numbers: Leahy & Sweller Exp 1: study better for novices, imagination better for the same children two weeks later as relative experts; Exp 2 replicated with stronger effects. Exact means not given in the review.
limits: Primary school, bus timetable and temperature graphs. Spreadsheet and HTML domains in the other two studies.
agent_relevance: Reversal inside the same learner over time: support level must follow current competence, not a fixed schedule.

source: Kalyuga (2010) Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue
finding: Editor summary of a five-paper special issue. Describes the theory (redundant guidance adds extraneous load for experts) and one partial field replication.
numbers: Salden et al.: in the lab, adaptive fading beat fixed fading and plain tutored problem solving on immediate and one-week delayed posttests. In the classroom, it replicated on the delayed posttest but not on the immediate posttest (high school geometry, Cognitive Tutor).
quote: The classroom study replicated this effect on the delayed posttest but not on the immediate posttest.
limits: Partial replication in the field. Editor is an effect proponent.
agent_relevance: Gains from adaptive fading may show only on delayed or transfer tests; an immediate-accuracy eval could miss them.

source: Salden, Aleven, Schwonke, Renkl (2009) Worked examples and tutored problem solving: redundant or synergistic forms of support?
finding: Two experiments (lab and classroom): standard Cognitive Tutor vs example-enhanced tutor with fixed fading vs adaptive fading.
numbers: Adaptive fading gave higher transfer on delayed posttests than the other two methods (per abstract; numbers not read).
limits: Abstract only, via OpenAlex. Fixed fading did not clearly beat plain tutoring.
agent_relevance: The gain came from adapting to the learner, not from fading itself. Fits a per-class gate.

source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters, Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity: a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect
finding: First formal meta-analysis. Low-prior-knowledge learners benefit from high-assistance instruction and high-prior-knowledge learners from low-assistance instruction. Robust but moderated.
numbers: From a search summary, not verified: 60 experiments, 5,924 participants, 176 effect sizes; low prior knowledge d=0.505 for high assistance; high prior knowledge d=-0.428 (favouring low assistance).
limits: Publisher page blocked (403), so numbers come from a secondary snippet. Evidence is weaker for younger students, humanities and language learning. Moderated by educational status and content domain.
agent_relevance: Best estimate so far: the reversal is real but medium-sized (about 0.4 to 0.5), not the 1.7 of the early cross-sectional review. Plan for modest, domain-dependent effects.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-shot in-context learning
finding: Many-shot prompting can help a lot but returns are not monotone: more examples can lower accuracy.
numbers: MATH500 with human solutions: gain up to about 125 examples, then decline. GPQA with ground-truth rationales: best at 125 shots (near Claude-3 Opus), degraded at 250 shots. Reinforced ICL (model-written rationales) plateaued near 25 shots, about 5% above human-rationale ICL, with no big drop at large counts.
quote: many-shot ICL achieves comparable or superior performance when using only problems compared to using problems with solutions
limits: Gemini 1.5 Pro. GPQA is small and noisy; the authors say they do not fully understand the declines.
agent_relevance: Library size has a peak. Solutions may be redundant for tasks the model already knows from pretraining (math), an expertise-reversal analogue. Model-made examples beat human ones at equal count.

source: Tang et al. (2025) The few-shot dilemma: over-prompting large language models
finding: Adding more relevant examples degraded some models. The best count depends on the model's long-context ability.
numbers: Software requirement classification (PROMISE, PURE). LLaMA-3.2-3B worsened significantly beyond 80 examples (hill-shaped macro F1). GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 showed no significant drop. DeepSeek-V3 gained from 120 to 160 examples. Best combined method beat the state of the art by 1% on functional vs non-functional classification.
limits: Narrow domain; weak models may be hurt by length, not by redundancy. A different cause from expertise reversal (context limits).
agent_relevance: Separate two causes of too-many-examples harm: capacity or length, and redundancy. Cap lesson count per class and measure.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) When correct demonstrations hurt: rethinking the role of exemplars in in-context learning
finding: Correct examples can reduce accuracy when they shift the model's evidence mix. Smaller models are more affected than larger ones.
numbers: SST-2: LLaMA-2-7B fell from 96.4% to 56.9% accuracy at 100% perturbed exemplars; LLaMA-3.1-8B from 98.2% to 66.0%. Math Medium split: LLaMA-3.1-8B -6.6%, 70B -1.4%. Hard split: Qwen2.5-14B -9.3%, 72B -4.9%. Recent large models stayed within about 2% of clean.
quote: correctness does not guarantee exemplar utility
limits: Perturbed exemplars are task-preserving rewrites, not redundant ones. Smaller models are the vulnerable ones: the opposite direction from expertise reversal (strong models are robust, not harmed).
agent_relevance: A correct example is not a safe example. Choose examples by measured utility on held-out items (G3), not by correctness. Stronger models tolerate bad examples better.

source: Hannan et al. (2026) On the difficulty of selecting few-shot examples for LLM-based vulnerability detection
finding: Choosing examples where the model errs (Learn-from-Mistakes) or near neighbours helped weaker models a lot and a stronger model little. Helped on some datasets, failed on others.
numbers: NodeMedic: Gemma-3-4b F1 0.574 zero-shot to 0.854 with nearest-neighbour examples. Random few-shot already gave GPT-5-mini F1 0.860; adaptive methods gave only a slight edge. On PrimeVul and SVENC nearest-neighbour examples left Qwen F1 at 0.104 and 0.075; Qwen zero-shot F1 was 0.000 on both. C and C++: little effect.
limits: Single-run GPT result; table text was garbled in extraction so only numbers quoted in the paper text are used. Mistake-targeted examples often pushed the model to predict one class (accuracy 0.500 hid it).
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of S0 (show examples on weak classes). The gain shrinks as the model gets stronger, and error-targeted examples can bias outputs: track F1 and class balance, not accuracy alone.

source: Authors not recorded (2025) Explainable sentiment analysis with DeepSeek-R1: performance, efficiency and few-shot learning
finding: A reasoning model needed far fewer examples than a non-reasoning one to reach the same ceiling.
numbers: IMDB binary: DeepSeek-R1 99.31% accuracy with 5 shots; GPT-4o needed 40 shots for the same 99.31%. GoEmotions 27-class: R1 45.33% (10 shots) vs GPT-4o 45.17% (10 shots). Optimal shots rise with task complexity: 5 to 20 on IMDB, 30 to 50 on Amazon 5-class.
limits: Optimal shot counts were picked on test curves; no variance reported. Different models, not one model at different skill levels.
agent_relevance: Stronger models saturate with fewer examples, and harder classes want more. Set lesson count by class difficulty.

source: Honda et al. (2025) Distilling many-shot in-context learning into a cheat sheet
finding: A short distilled summary matched many-shot prompting at far fewer tokens. Mid-shot settings showed sudden drops on some tasks.
numbers: Cheat sheet matched or beat many-shot ICL and matched retrieval-based ICL on reasoning tasks. Removing a world-knowledge section from one cheat sheet raised accuracy from 87.0 to 89.7. Many-shot prompts used about 45,000 to 70,000 tokens.
limits: Full tables not extracted. The cheat sheet is built from the training demos by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Supports condensing lessons into rules per class rather than piling up raw examples, and editing out parts that hurt.

source: Liu et al. (2025) What makes in-context learning effective for mathematical reasoning
finding: Few-shot demonstrations can bring negative performance in math reasoning. Effect depends on similarity to the query and on stability of the model's inference on the demonstration.
numbers: Theory plus experiments on three benchmarks and two LLMs. Their method LMS3 includes a rejection step that filters unsuitable demonstrations and improved all datasets (exact numbers not extracted). Fig 1 compares zero-shot and one-shot accuracy.
quote: few-shot demonstrations can sometimes bring negative performance
limits: Only the abstract and figure caption were read in detail; numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: A rejection gate for lessons: if the model already solves the item stably zero-shot, do not add an example. This is the code-level version of expertise reversal.

source: Kalyuga (2007) theory section: why reversal happens
finding: Explanation: experts must cross-reference redundant guidance with their own schema, which adds extraneous load. Germane-load activities (self-explanation, imagination) can overload novices and help experts.
numbers: No pooled number. Full reversals appeared in controlled longitudinal studies and also in cross-sectional ones; partial reversals (non-significant for one group but a significant interaction) were more common.
limits: Rival accounts (aptitude-treatment interaction, Cronbach 1967; element interactivity) mostly redescribe the same data; no study in the review separates them.
agent_relevance: The LLM mechanism may differ: no working-memory limit in the same sense. Treat the human theory as a design hint, not a mechanism.

source: Kalyuga (2007) on weaker cases: Tuovinen & Sweller (1999), Kalyuga & Sweller (2004) Exp 3
finding: Not every case reverses. Guided worked examples beat discovery for novices; for knowledgeable learners there was no difference (Tuovinen & Sweller) or a lean to problem solving (Kalyuga & Sweller).
numbers: Kalyuga & Sweller 2004 Exp 3: median split on a rapid pretest, coordinate geometry; significant interaction between knowledge level and format. Tuovinen & Sweller: no condition difference for higher-knowledge students.
limits: Median splits discard information. Partial reversal is the common case, so the main claim is an interaction.
agent_relevance: Expect the common result on strong classes to be 'no gain', not always 'harm'. The cost of adding lessons there is tokens and risk, with no benefit.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) many-shot: GSM8K transfer and unsupervised ICL
finding: Examples with only problems matched examples with solutions on MATH. Model-generated solutions transferred better to GSM8K.
numbers: Reinforced ICL with MATH prompts outperformed ground-truth-solution ICL and Unsupervised ICL on GSM8K at 25 or more shots. Unsupervised ICL on GPQA showed no systematic trend (small noisy set).
limits: One model family; one benchmark per condition.
agent_relevance: When the model already knows the skill, the solution text matters less than the problem distribution. Evidence for dropping solution text on strong classes.

source: Tang et al. (2025) example selection methods
finding: TF-IDF and stratified selection beat random and embedding-based selection and avoided over-prompting.
numbers: TF-IDF plus stratification reached the best score with fewer examples per model. F1 values around 90 on the relabeled PROMISE set; Gemma-3-4B and the two LLaMA models declined dramatically after their peak. Exact grid not extracted.
limits: Peaks chosen on a validation split of one small dataset (80-20 split).
agent_relevance: Per-model, per-class tuning of lesson count is needed; do not fix a global count.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) exemplar position effect
finding: Small models over-weight recent exemplars; large models spread attention to early clean ones.
numbers: Accuracy with perturbed exemplars placed last: 92.3%, 77.6%, 58.1% at three ratios, vs 94.7%, 88.2%, 72.9% under random placement (small model).
limits: Single small-model family; the attention analysis is descriptive.
agent_relevance: Put the most reliable lesson nearest the query; order matters most for weaker models.

source: R1 sentiment study: size and distillation
finding: Model size changes how many examples help.
numbers: Binary IMDB accuracy: 8B 95.17%, 14B 97.47%, 32B 96.55%, 70B 97.93%, full R1 99.31%. Qwen-based 32B beat Llama-based 70B by 6.69 percentage points on a 5-class task.
limits: Optimal shot counts differ by model (5 to 40) and were chosen at the optimum on the test set, so numbers are optimistic.
agent_relevance: Shot count is a per-model parameter; a stronger model reaches the same accuracy from fewer examples.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025) moderators and robustness
finding: Reported moderators: educational status and content domain. Evidence is less clear for younger students and for humanities and language learning.
numbers: Secondary summary only; no moderator coefficients seen.
limits: Not opened. Needs verification from the full text.
agent_relevance: If domain moderates the effect, class-level routing for the agent should be tested per domain, not assumed.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) many-shot: overriding pretraining bias
finding: With enough examples a model can override a wrong prior (flipped or abstract labels in sentiment), and performance rises with more shots.
numbers: Sentiment analysis (Financial PhraseBank): accuracy typically improves with more shots; flipped and abstract labels eventually approach default-label performance.
quote: many-shot ICL can overcome pre-training biases
limits: Applies where the model's prior is wrong. More examples help here, the opposite of redundancy.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: where the model is weak because its prior is wrong, more examples help a lot. Show lessons exactly there.

source: Hannan et al. (2026) model-strength gap
finding: Open small models gained much more from adaptive examples than the stronger closed model.
numbers: Conclusion: open-source models do worse under baseline few-shot but gain substantially from combined methods and in some cases approach GPT-5-mini. GPT-5-mini baseline F1 was already high on NodeMedic (0.860).
limits: Single GPT run; datasets differ widely in difficulty.
agent_relevance: Another match for the novice-gains, expert-flat pattern in LLMs, but without a negative expert effect.
